# DNA binding motifs and gene regulation

A motif is the sequence of nucleotides that a DNA binding protein,
such as a transcription factor, prefers to bind. As we discussed in
class, "binding" here means that amino acid residues of the protein
make favorable contacts with nucleotides in the major groove of the
DNA double helix, and some sequences of letters make for better
contacts than others.

Transcription factor motifs are usually 6-20 bp long. The binding
isn't perfectly specific: a protein will bind to a family of similar
sequences, some more strongly than others. So instead of a single
sequence, we describe a motif with a position probability matrix,
which gives the probability of each nucleotide at each position of
the motif. You will also see the position weight matrix (PWM), which
is the log of these probabilities divided by the background frequency
of each nucleotide. A positive value in the PWM means that nucleotide
is more common at that position of the motif than in the genome
overall.

Transcription factors find their target genes by binding to
instances of their motif in cis-regulatory elements (CREs), such as
promoters and enhancers. A CRE typically has binding sites for a
number of transcription factors, which together determine whether
and when the nearby gene is transcribed. A short motif will also
match by chance at a huge number of places in the genome, and most of
these are never bound, for example because they are in closed
chromatin. This is why we usually look for motifs in regions where
there is experimental evidence of binding, such as ChIP-seq peaks,
rather than scanning the whole genome.

For most transcription factors, we can't yet predict the motif from
the protein sequence or structure alone. AlphaFold 3 and similar
tools can model protein-DNA complexes, but getting an accurate motif
out of these is still an open problem. So we learn motifs from data.

The setup is: we have a set of DNA sequences (ChIP-seq peaks, or the
promoters of genes that respond to some stimulus), and we want to find
a sequence pattern that shows up in many of them. What makes this
hard:

- We don't know which windows of each sequence contain the motif.
- We don't know the motif itself.
- The background sequence isn't uniformly random. If the genome is
  AT-rich, an AT-rich pattern will look common just because its
  letters are common.
- The motif can be on either strand.
- Some sequences won't contain the motif at all.
- The sequences may contain motifs for more than one transcription
  factor.

The model below deals with the first three, and ignores the rest to
keep things simple. EM is a good fit here, with the windows that
contain the motif as the latent variable. Keep in mind that what EM
finds are candidate binding sites, patterns that are over-represented
relative to the background, and these still need to be checked
against other evidence.

The code below is a simplified simulation and model, following the
setup of the MEME method, which proposed EM for motif finding:

*MEME: discovering and analyzing DNA and protein sequence motifs* -
[link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1538909/)

Before we get started, note that EM is not the only way to find these
motifs. Another, seemingly more direct approach, would be to tabulate
all the k-mers for a value of k that is large, but less than the
length of the motif we are looking for. If we look across sequences
which should occasionally contain the motif, we will likely find sets
of k-mers that occur more than we would expect in "background" DNA
sequences.

# The model

MEME breaks every sequence into overlapping windows the same width as
the motif, and asks of each window: is this a motif or is this
background? This is a mixture of two components, just like the
mixture of distributions from before:

* The motif component is a matrix $\theta$ with 4 rows and as many
  columns as the motif is wide. Each column gives the probabilities of
  A,C,G,T at that position of the motif. This is the position
  probability matrix from above, and $\log(\theta / \theta_{bg})$ is
  the PWM.
* The background component is a single vector $\theta_{bg}$ of
  nucleotide probabilities, the same for every position.
* $\lambda$ is the mixing proportion, the probability that a given
  window is a motif.

The hidden variable $Z_i$ is 1 if window *i* is a motif and 0 if it
is background. This sets up a problem that can be tackled with EM: if
we knew the motif, we could find which windows are motifs, and if we
knew which windows are motifs, we could easily determine the motif. We
start with neither.

The background component is essential. Without it, the model has no
way to say "this window doesn't look like the motif", and it has to
explain every window as a motif. It also lets us account for the fact
that the four nucleotides are not in equal abundance in genomes: a
window full of common nucleotides should not look like a motif just
because those nucleotides are common.

The over-simplifications we will make here, which result in an
unrealistic simulation, but are useful for pedagogical purposes:

* Each DNA sequence will be the same length. In reality, we often will
  have experimental data that a protein binds to a location, but each
  genomic range will have a different width.
* Each DNA sequence will contain the motif exactly once. With
  experimental data, a number of the locations where we find a protein
  bound to DNA might not contain that protein's motif. It is possible
  that the protein we are interested in is bound to another protein
  that is bound to DNA, so our protein is not making direct contact
  with DNA through its motif.
* I will only look on one strand of the DNA, instead of on both
  strands.
* We will know the width of the motif.

# Simulation

I begin by defining some parameters and simulating our motif that we
want to find. Here I use numbers 1-4 to represent nucleotides A,C,G,T.

```{r}
n <- 300 # number of DNA sequences
l <- 100 # number of nucleotides for each sequence
motif_len <- 10 # the length of the true motif
set.seed(5)
motif <- sample(1:4, motif_len, TRUE)
motif
```

Now we will embed the motif into some DNA sequences, which here are
rows of a matrix *x*. The vector *z* keeps track of the start
position of the motif in each sequence.

```{r}
x <- matrix(sample(1:4, n * l, TRUE),nrow=n)
z <- sample(l - motif_len + 1, n, TRUE)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  x[i, z[i] + 0:(motif_len-1)] <- motif
}
head(z)
x[1,z[1] + 0:(motif_len-1)]
```

The sequence motifs of a DNA binding protein vary across the genome:
there are always some, and often many, positions within a motif which
allow for a variety of nucleotides. To mimic this, we replace 20% of
the nucleotides with a random nucleotide. As the random nucleotide is
the same as the original one quarter of the time, about 15% of
positions change.

```{r}
noise <- 0.2
set.seed(1)
mutate_pos <- matrix(runif(n * l) < noise, nrow=n)
x[mutate_pos] <- sample(1:4, sum(mutate_pos), TRUE)
x[1,z[1] + 0:(motif_len-1)]
motif
```

Now we redefine the data as MEME does, with one row per window. Each
sequence contributes `n_win` windows, so the window starting at
position `p` of sequence `i` is in row `(i-1) * n_win + p`.

```{r}
w <- motif_len # width of the windows and of theta
n_win <- l - w + 1 # number of windows per sequence
win <- matrix(nrow=n * n_win, ncol=w)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  for (p in seq_len(n_win)) {
    win[(i-1) * n_win + p,] <- x[i, p + 0:(w-1)]
  }
}
dim(win)
# rows of `win` that hold the true motifs
motif_idx <- z + 0:(n-1) * n_win
```

We can look at the windows holding the true motifs to see how much
they vary (A,C,G,T in green, blue, orange, red):

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
cols <- c("green3","blue","orange","red")
pheatmap::pheatmap(win[motif_idx,], cluster_rows=FALSE,
                   cluster_cols=FALSE, show_rownames=FALSE,
                   color=cols, breaks=0:4 + .5, legend=FALSE)
```

# One step of EM

The likelihood of a window under the motif component is the product,
over positions, of the probability in $\theta$ of the nucleotide we
see at that position. Under the background component it is the
product of the background probabilities of its nucleotides. We
estimate $\theta_{bg}$ once, from the overall frequency of each
nucleotide, and hold it fixed.

```{r}
lik_motif <- function(snip, theta) {
  prod(sapply(1:4, function(k) prod(theta[k, snip == k])))
}
lik_bg <- function(snip, theta_bg) {
  prod(theta_bg[snip])
}
theta_bg <- tabulate(x, 4) / length(x)
theta_bg
```

We start with a random guess $\theta^0$, where each column sums to 1,
and with $\lambda^0$ equal to one motif per sequence.

```{r}
random_theta <- function(w) {
  theta <- matrix(runif(w*4), ncol=w)
  sweep(theta, 2, colSums(theta), "/")
}
set.seed(3)
theta <- random_theta(w)
round(theta, 2)
lambda <- 1/n_win
```

In the E-step, the conditional probability that window *i* is a motif
is the familiar ratio from mixture models:

$$
P(Z_i = 1 | X_i, \theta^t, \lambda^t) =
\frac{\lambda^t \, P(X_i | \theta^t)}{\lambda^t \, P(X_i | \theta^t) +
(1 - \lambda^t) \, P(X_i | \theta_{bg})}
$$

Let's calculate this for the first window of the first sequence.

```{r}
snip <- win[1,]
snip
f_motif <- lambda * lik_motif(snip, theta)
f_bg <- (1 - lambda) * lik_bg(snip, theta_bg)
f_motif / (f_motif + f_bg)
```

To compute the motif likelihood for all windows at once, it is much
faster to loop over the `w` columns than over the many rows of `win`:
for column `j`, `theta[cbind(win[,j], j)]` picks out the probability
of the nucleotide observed at position `j` in every window. This gives
the same answer as applying `lik_motif` to each row:

```{r}
lik_motif_all <- function(win, theta) {
  lik <- rep(1, nrow(win))
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(win))) {
    lik <- lik * theta[cbind(win[,j], j)]
  }
  lik
}
all.equal(lik_motif_all(win, theta),
          apply(win, 1, lik_motif, theta=theta))
```

As the background likelihood of each window doesn't change, we only
need to compute it once. We then compute the conditional probability
for all windows:

```{r}
lik_bg_win <- apply(win, 1, lik_bg, theta_bg=theta_bg)
f_motif <- lambda * lik_motif_all(win, theta)
f_bg <- (1 - lambda) * lik_bg_win
post_motif <- f_motif / (f_motif + f_bg)
summary(post_motif)
```

In the M-step, we maximize the expected log likelihood, where the
expectation is over the conditional distribution of *Z* given *X* and
the current parameters. The update for $\lambda$ is the average of
the conditional probabilities. The update for each column of $\theta$
is a weighted frequency of the nucleotides at that position, where
each window is weighted by its probability of being a motif. Note
that if we knew exactly which windows were motifs (`post_motif` all
0 or 1), this would simply count the nucleotides at each position
across the motifs.

```{r}
lambda <- mean(post_motif)
counts <- t(sapply(1:4, function(k) colSums(post_motif * (win == k))))
theta <- sweep(counts, 2, colSums(counts), "/")
round(theta, 2)
```

# Running EM

Now we put these two pieces together within a loop. We also keep
track of the log likelihood at each iteration, which EM should never
decrease, and the estimate of $\theta$ at each iteration, so we can
plot it.

```{r}
meme_em <- function(theta, lambda, niter) {
  loglik <- numeric(niter)
  theta_hist <- list(theta)
  for (t in seq_len(niter)) {
    # E-step: probability that each window is a motif
    f_motif <- lambda * lik_motif_all(win, theta)
    f_bg <- (1 - lambda) * lik_bg_win
    loglik[t] <- sum(log(f_motif + f_bg)) # log lik at theta^(t-1)
    post_motif <- f_motif / (f_motif + f_bg)
    # M-step: update the mixing proportion and the motif matrix
    lambda <- mean(post_motif)
    counts <- t(sapply(1:4, function(k) colSums(post_motif * (win == k))))
    theta <- sweep(counts, 2, colSums(counts), "/")
    theta_hist[[t + 1]] <- theta
  }
  list(theta=theta, lambda=lambda, post_motif=post_motif,
       loglik=loglik, theta_hist=theta_hist)
}
```

EM finds a local maximum of the likelihood, and which one depends on
where we start. So, like MEME, we try a number of starting points and
keep the best.

```{r}
n_starts <- 20
niter <- 60
fits <- lapply(seq_len(n_starts), function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  meme_em(random_theta(w), lambda=1/n_win, niter=niter)
})
```

The log likelihood increases over iterations for every start (one
line per start), but the starts end up at different values. We plot
the log likelihood relative to the highest value seen across all
starts, so the top of the plot is 0 (a likelihood ratio of 1 with the
best start):

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=5}
ll <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "loglik")
matplot(ll[-1,] - max(ll), type="l", lty=1, col=1:n_starts,
        xlab="iteration", ylab="log likelihood relative to best")
```

Some starts converge to a shifted version of the motif. For each
start, we can find the window in each sequence with the highest
probability of being a motif, and compare it to the true start
position `z`. The most common offset between the chosen window and
`z` tells us how far the motif was shifted. We then count how many of
the true motif locations were recovered, allowing for that shift.

```{r}
summarize_fit <- function(fit) {
  post_mat <- matrix(fit$post_motif, nrow=n, byrow=TRUE)
  offset <- apply(post_mat, 1, which.max) - z
  shift <- as.numeric(names(which.max(table(offset))))
  c(loglik=fit$loglik[niter],
    shift=shift,
    recovered=sum(offset == shift))
}
res <- t(sapply(fits, summarize_fit))
res
```

Some starts end up at the same values, so we jitter the points
slightly, and label each size of shift (left or right) once:

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=5}
set.seed(1)
jit_x <- jitter(res[,"recovered"], amount=2)
jit_y <- jitter(res[,"loglik"] - max(res[,"loglik"]), amount=10)
plot(jit_x, jit_y, xlim=range(jit_x) + c(-5, 15),
     xlab="true motif locations recovered (allowing for shift)",
     ylab="final log likelihood relative to best")
abs_shift <- abs(res[,"shift"])
# one label per size of shift, to the right of its group of points
lab_x <- tapply(jit_x, abs_shift, max)
lab_y <- tapply(jit_y, abs_shift, mean)
text(lab_x, lab_y, labels=paste("shift", names(lab_x)), pos=4, cex=.8)
```

The starts with no shift have the highest log likelihood and recover
the most motif locations. The larger the shift, the lower the log
likelihood, and the fewer of the motif locations are recovered, even
after accounting for the shift.

To see this, we define a function to draw an estimate of $\theta$ as
a row of squares, colored by the most likely nucleotide at each
position, and more transparent when that nucleotide's probability is
closer to 1/4. The argument `shift` moves the squares left or right.

```{r}
drawTheta <- function(theta, y, shift=0) {
  theta_max <- apply(theta, 2, which.max)
  theta_max_p <- apply(theta, 2, max)
  cols_alpha <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(theta)), function(i) {
    adjustcolor(cols[theta_max[i]],(theta_max_p[i] - .25)/.75)
  })
  points(seq_len(ncol(theta)) + shift, rep(y,ncol(theta)),
         col=cols_alpha, pch=15, cex=2)
}
```

Drawing the final $\theta$ from each start, moved by its shift so that
it lines up with the true motif at the bottom, with starts ordered by
their final log likelihood (highest at the top):

```{r, fig.width=7, fig.height=8, message=FALSE}
library(rafalib)
ord <- order(res[,"loglik"])
nullplot(min(res[,"shift"]), w + max(res[,"shift"]) + 1, -1, n_starts,
         xlab="position relative to true motif",
         ylab="starts, ordered by log likelihood")
points(seq_len(w), rep(-1,w), col=cols[motif], pch=15, cex=2)
for (k in seq_len(n_starts)) {
  drawTheta(fits[[ord[k]]]$theta, k, shift=res[ord[k],"shift"])
}
abline(v=c(.5, w + .5), lty=2)
```

All of the starts found the same motif. But a $\theta$ shifted by $s$
positions only covers $10 - s$ positions of the motif (inside the
dashed lines). Its other $s$ columns line up with the random sequence
next to the motif, so they are close to the background frequencies
(the faded squares), and explain the data no better than the
background component does. Each position of the motif that falls
outside of $\theta$ is information we are not using, and so the
likelihood is lower.

Why doesn't EM fix the shift? A shifted $\theta$ is a local maximum
that is hard to escape: moving it one position over would mean
passing through worse values of the likelihood. MEME deals with this
by trying many starting points (derived from substrings of the data
rather than random values) and by explicitly trying shifted versions
of the motif. Here, we simply keep the start with the highest log
likelihood.

```{r}
best_start <- which.max(ll[niter,])
best <- fits[[best_start]]
round(best$theta, 2)
motif
```

We can follow the estimates of $\theta$ over the iterations for this
start, for the first 20 iterations. The random initialization has no
clear motif, and for the
first few iterations not much happens. Then a few positions that
happen to agree with the motif start to pull the conditional
probabilities of the true motif windows upward, and the rest of the
motif fills in over a few iterations.

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=7}
n_show <- 20 # the best start converges well before this
nullplot(0, w + 1, -1, n_show,
         xlab="position in motif", ylab="iteration")
points(seq_len(w), rep(-1,w), col=cols[motif], pch=15, cex=2)
for (t in 0:n_show) {
  drawTheta(best$theta_hist[[t + 1]], t)
}
```

The estimate of $\lambda$, converted to motifs per sequence, should be
close to 1:

```{r}
best$lambda * n_win
```

A few remaining differences from MEME: MEME uses pseudocounts (a
Dirichlet prior) so that no entry of $\theta$ becomes exactly 0, it
searches both strands, it allows for sequences without the motif, it
searches over the width of the motif, and it accounts for the fact
that overlapping windows can't both be motifs. Here we treated the
windows as independent, which they are not.

# Appendix: Why the weighted frequency maximizes our target

In the M-step we said that we maximize the expected log likelihood,
without writing it down. Here we show that the weighted frequencies
used above are exactly the maximizer. Let $x_{ij}$ be the nucleotide
at position $j$ of window $i$, and let $N$ be the number of windows.
The log likelihood of the complete data, if we knew which windows were
motifs, is:

$$
\log P(X, Z | \theta, \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^N Z_i \left[\log \lambda +
\sum_{j=1}^w \sum_{k=1}^4 1(x_{ij}=k) \log \theta_{kj}\right] +
(1 - Z_i) \left[\log(1-\lambda) + \log P(X_i | \theta_{bg})\right]
$$

This is linear in the $Z_i$. So the expectation over the conditional
distribution of $Z$ given $X$ and the current parameters just replaces
each $Z_i$ with its conditional probability
$r_i = P(Z_i = 1 | X_i, \theta^t, \lambda^t)$, which is `post_motif`
in the code:

$$
Q(\theta, \lambda | \theta^t, \lambda^t) = \sum_{i=1}^N r_i \left[\log \lambda +
\sum_{j=1}^w \sum_{k=1}^4 1(x_{ij}=k) \log \theta_{kj}\right] +
(1 - r_i) \left[\log(1-\lambda) + \log P(X_i | \theta_{bg})\right]
$$

No integration over $Z$ is needed in practice, because of this
linearity. The terms involving $\theta_{bg}$ are held fixed, so they
do not affect the maximization. The remaining terms separate into a
part with only $\lambda$ and a part with only $\theta$.

For $\lambda$, we maximize $\sum_i r_i \log \lambda + (1 - r_i)
\log(1-\lambda)$. Setting the derivative to zero:

$$
\frac{\sum_i r_i}{\lambda} - \frac{\sum_i (1 - r_i)}{1 - \lambda} = 0
\quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i r_i
$$

which is `mean(post_motif)`.

For $\theta$, define the weighted counts
$c_{kj} = \sum_i r_i \, 1(x_{ij}=k)$. We maximize
$\sum_j \sum_k c_{kj} \log \theta_{kj}$ subject to each column summing
to 1. With a Lagrange multiplier $\mu_j$ for each column, we set the
derivative with respect to $\theta_{kj}$ to zero:

$$
\frac{c_{kj}}{\theta_{kj}} - \mu_j = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad
\theta_{kj} = \frac{c_{kj}}{\mu_j}
$$

The constraint $\sum_k \theta_{kj} = 1$ gives $\mu_j = \sum_k c_{kj}$,
so

$$
\theta_{kj} = \frac{c_{kj}}{\sum_{k'} c_{k'j}}
$$

This is the weighted frequency of nucleotide $k$ at position $j$, the
`counts` matrix divided by its column sums in the code. When every
$r_i$ is 0 or 1, it reduces to the ordinary maximum likelihood
estimate: counting the nucleotides at each position across the windows
that are motifs.
